title: Kingsford Heights, Indiana: the wartime town that stood empty, and what the plant next door left in the ground
sourcing_note: Second blind check of the remake, Nov. 16, 2026: every line supported; fixes: the chemicals line now says 'Defense Department cleanup data from 2015 listed lead, arsenic, mercury and TNT in soil and groundwater at sites on the old plant grounds, outside town' (ProPublica, 2017, from DoD data last updated in 2015; the checker found the Army Corps' mapped munitions site in the Kingsbury Fish & Wildlife Area, miles from the town center, and the same Corps data shows both sites closed in Sept. 2017 with the rest of the plant's work folded into one project still in investigation, target 2036); 'explosives like' and 'of them' and 'now' cut for length; the first cut-away's patch now sits under the plant's fenced grounds, beside its buildings, so it can't read as the town; the end card shows the wildlife area at night, not the town's houses, so 'IT COULD BE NEXT' can't read as the town being contaminated; credits name ProPublica 2017 with the 2015 data and drop Wikipedia and the unchecked DHPA survey. Blind check of the remake, Nov. 16, 2026 (script, on-screen text and pictures only), and the fixes: 'Defense Department cleanup records list ... in its soil and groundwater' became 'have listed ... in soil and groundwater on the old plant grounds' (ProPublica's page is built from fiscal 2015 Defense Environmental Restoration Program data, so 'have listed' and the credits say 2015; the records are about the plant grounds, not the town); 'Part of the old plant' became 'Part of that land'; 'packed up and' was dropped (only the Green Bay record says the houses were packaged). Pictures: the dark patches now sink straight down and stay put (no source shows the contamination moving), nothing is built over them (the records don't say the plant buildings were the source), the plant stands far off in the first cut-away, and the second shows two patches, as ProPublica lists two active sites. The Defense Department's FY2025 table (posted June 2026) puts the plant's 4 IRP sites at response complete (2009) and its 1 munitions site at 2046 (used only in the Kingsbury short). REMADE Nov. 16, 2026 at Scoop's request ('remake kingsbury and kingsford heights to include how toxic and contaminated from the munitions plant it is'). The ghost-town story is kept (lines 0-4 shortened from the checked version; 'its streets were laid out in long curves' and 'empty lots still dot' dropped for time). Added: the plant next door left contamination. The contamination facts are about the old plant grounds, not the town of Kingsford Heights: no source found reports contamination in the town itself, so nothing is drawn under a house and the narration says 'the plant next door' and 'its soil and groundwater'. 'Defense Department cleanup records list lead, arsenic, mercury and explosives like TNT in its soil and groundwater': ProPublica's Bombs in Your Backyard page for the Kingsbury Ordnance Plant (FUDS IN59799F357000), built from Defense Environmental Restoration Program data the Pentagon released; both active sites list TNT, arsenic, mercury and lead in soil and groundwater (03HTRW groundwater: TNT 0.71 ug/L, mercury 230, arsenic 3400, lead 78,500; 04OEW soil: TNT 0.53 mg/kg, arsenic 163, mercury 167, lead 2,000). One record set, so the line names who keeps it. The Army Corps' FUDS program covers DoD-generated contamination, which is why 'the plant ... left' is fair. 'Part of the old plant is a state wildlife area now. Its map marks some spots: Contaminated Area. No Trespassing.': the DNR's Kingsbury FWA map (2022) and its 2025 hunt map both carry the legend 'Contaminated Area/No Trespassing'; the 2022 rules say contaminated areas are off limits at all times; the DNR says the area is a remnant of the old plant. The sign is drawn with those legend words; the DNR's real sign design is not known, so it is a plain yellow sign. Left out: the Fisher-Calo Superfund site (its waste came from a solvent company in the 1970s, not the plant: kept for the Kingsbury short, where that is said); drinking-water wells (ProPublica's note that wide well spacing gives 'no conclusive evidence' contamination isn't moving off site is one record, possibly dated, and could alarm residents without a second source); cleanup dates. Earlier checked note (Nov. 16): Requested town (Scoop, Nov. 16, 2026). No ghost legend or dark event with two sources was found for Kingsford Heights itself (the Kingsbury Ordnance Plant had no major accidents, IPM and Places That Were; the 1965 tornado and the plant itself already ran), so this is eerie history: the government's near-empty wartime town. Not the Nov. 7/15 Kingsbury plant short's story (that one only said 'a whole new town went up'). Occupancy: 'only around 300' rests on Towne Post and the History Museum (same wording, one source); the 1940s 'New Deal Ghost Town' story ('Only [n] families moved in', 'abandoned') is the second, so the narration says 'most of them stood empty', no number. The headline card uses the real headline words; its paper and date come from the Utah Digital Newspapers record (see the check below). Houses moved: 185 to Evansville's Diamond Villa (Clio) and 100 to Green Bay (Wisconsin Historical Society): 'hundreds'. 'Packed up' follows Green Bay's 'package the houses'. No picture shows how they travelled (the crate sits on skids). Rename date left out (sources disagree: 1942 vs. after the purchase). 'Empty lots' rests on the DHPA survey via Wikipedia. The streets: Towne Post ('wagon wheel') and the DHPA survey ('curvilinear arrangement'); no town plan is drawn (see the check below). Independent check Nov. 16 (blind, script/text/pictures only): 'Nearly 3,000 houses went up' became 'Thousands of homes went up' (sources split between 3,000 planned, 2,974 built in the 1944 story, and 'more than 2,600 dormitories, trailers, and prefabricated homes'); the headline card now names the paper, the Garfield County News (Panguitch, Utah), Sept. 28, 1944, as the checker read the Utah Digital Newspapers record (neighboring record 3301869 is the same paper's Oct. 12, 1944 issue); 'bought the town' became 'bought the land from the government and incorporated the town' (town website; Wikipedia); the aerial ring drawing was dropped (no map could be checked from here) and 'curved in rings around a town center' became 'laid out in long curves, not a grid' (Towne Post's 'wagon wheel' rather than a grid; the DHPA survey's 'curvilinear arrangement'); first label 1940s so the dark street isn't read as today. New homes are filling some lots (Century Communities listings), so the line says empty lots 'still dot' the streets, not that they line them. Second check Nov. 16: all four revised lines supported; the card drops '(UTAH)', which isn't printed on the scan (the paper is Panguitch's Garfield County News, per the Utah Digital Newspapers record, item 3301756 in issue 3301678, p. 8).

beats.text: Thousands of homes went up, and most stood empty. This is Kingsford Heights.
beats.label: LAPORTE COUNTY, 1940s
beats.credit: The History Museum, South Bend; Garfield County News, 1944

beats.text: In 1942, the government built it for workers at the Kingsbury Ordnance Plant next door. It was first called Victory City.
beats.label: KINGSBURY ORDNANCE PLANT
beats.credit: The History Museum; Indiana Public Media; Town of Kingsford Heights

beats.text: Many workers kept their own homes, and a 1944 headline called it a New Deal ghost town.
beats.credit: The History Museum; Towne Post; Garfield County News, Sept. 28, 1944

beats.text: Hundreds of houses were shipped off to other cities.
beats.credit: Clio (Diamond Villa, Evansville); Wisconsin Historical Society

beats.text: The families who stayed bought the land from the government and incorporated the town.
beats.label: KINGSFORD HEIGHTS
beats.credit: Town of Kingsford Heights; Towne Post

beats.text: But the plant next door left something in the ground.
beats.label: THE PLANT NEXT DOOR
beats.credit: ProPublica 2017 (Defense Dept. data, 2015); Army Corps of Engineers

beats.text: Defense Department cleanup data from 2015 listed lead, arsenic, mercury and TNT in soil and groundwater at sites on the old plant grounds, outside town.
beats.label: THE OLD PLANT GROUNDS

beats.text: Part of that land is a state wildlife area. Its map marks some spots: Contaminated Area. No Trespassing.
beats.label: KINGSBURY FISH & WILDLIFE AREA
beats.credit: Indiana DNR, Kingsbury Fish & Wildlife Area maps (2022, 2025)

beats.text: Comment your town, and it could be next.

sources.what: 'Initially dubbed "Victory City," planning for the town had begun alongside planning of the ordnance plant. Construction was underway for nearly 3,000 houses, on 775 acres of former farmland, in 1942.' Most houses one-story bungalows; layout 'a sort of "wagon wheel," circular pattern' with municipal services at the center; many workers 'preferred to commute from their own homes'; postwar reports indicated 'only around 300 of the homes were actually occupied during World War II'; residents purchased the town from the U.S. government; incorporated 1956.
sources.who: Jeff Kenney, 'Victory City', Towne Post (Lakes Region), April 2022

sources.what: 'Initially named "Victory City," ... Construction of nearly 3,000 on 775 acres began in 1942.' 'Workers rented the newly built bungalows from the government; numerous workers still commuted to Kingsbury from their own homes, and postwar news reports showed that only around 300 of the newly built homes were occupied during World War II.' (Wording close to Towne Post's: counted as one source with it for the occupancy figure.)
sources.who: The History Museum (South Bend), 'Indiana and Another World War'

sources.what: Headline 'NEW DEAL GHOST TOWN': 'acre tract of rich Indiana farm land purchased by the government from 14 farmers covered with 2974 war [houses]'; '18 miles of streets'; the Defense Housing Co. 'decided a new city should be built' for an anticipated workforce near the Army's shell loading plant; 'Only [OCR drops the number] families moved in'; 'Kingsford Heights was abandoned and placed on the liquidation list'. The paper's name and date are not shown on the page.
'Kingsford Heights consisted of more than 2,600 dormitories, trailers, and prefabricated homes.'
sources.who: Indiana Public Media, Moment of Indiana History, 'The Kingsbury Ordnance Plant' (after Katherine Turk, Indiana Magazine of History, 2012)

sources.what: Diamond Villa, established 1944: 'A total of 185 prefabricated housing units were relocated from Kingsford Heights in LaPorte County, Indiana.'

Green Bay Housing Authority bought 100 houses 'constructed for and used by defense industry workers at Kingsford Heights, Indiana' from the Federal Public Housing Authority; Greene and Gust Construction got a contract 'to package the houses in Kingsford Heights, Indiana, and to relocate and erect the houses in Green Bay'; first erected 1946, all built and sold to veterans by August 1947.
sources.who: Wisconsin Historical Society, Property Record HI245038

sources.what: Federal planners created a village near the plant, originally Victory City; original plans 3,000 homes; remaining residents purchased the land from the government and incorporated the town; the town boundary includes the entire planned community, 'even encompassing lots without houses' (citing the Indiana DHPA survey 'Calumet.pdf'). 2020 population 1,335.
sources.who: Wikipedia, 'Kingsford Heights, Indiana' (citing Indiana Division of Historic Preservation and Archaeology, Residential Planning and Development in Indiana 1940-1973 survey)

sources.what: Kingsbury Ordnance Plant (FUDS IN59799F357000): 6 hazardous sites, highest risk 'High'; active site 03HTRW: groundwater (High) with TNT 0.71 ug/L, RDX 39.0, mercury 230.0, arsenic 3400.0, lead 78500.0 ug/L; soil (Medium) arsenic 11.1, lead 14.8 mg/kg; active site 04OEW (unexploded munitions and ordnance area): soil (High) TNT 0.53, RDX 4.17, HMX 2480, arsenic 163.0, mercury 167.0, lead 2000.0 mg/kg; groundwater (Medium) arsenic 26.2, RDX 39.0 ug/L; final cleanup action Sep. 2040, monitoring until Sep. 2072; land: about 7,100 acres in the Kingsbury Fish and Wildlife Area, about 5,000 commercial/industrial; Fisher-Calo Superfund site on part of the former DoD-owned Kingsbury Industrial Development Park. Cost figures updated Dec. 5, 2017.
sources.who: ProPublica, Bombs in Your Backyard (Defense Environmental Restoration Program data obtained from the Department of Defense)

sources.what: The Formerly Used Defense Sites program is how the Corps responds to DoD-generated contamination and munitions that remained on a property when it was transferred.
sources.who: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Formerly Used Defense Sites (FUDS) program pages (archived)

sources.what: Map legend 'Contaminated Area/No Trespassing'; rules: 'Contaminated areas are off limits at all times'; 'Kingsbury is a remnant of the old Kingsbury Ordinance Plant, which produced shells, cartridges and mortar rounds for World War II and the Korean conflict.'
sources.who: Indiana DNR, Kingsbury Fish & Wildlife Area map and rules (05/2022)

sources.what: Map legend 'Contaminated Area/No Trespassing'; 'Kingsbury is a remnant of the old Kingsbury Ordnance Plant'; deeded to Indiana in 1965.
sources.who: Indiana DNR, Kingsbury FWA 2025 waterfowl draw information

sources.what: The Fisher-Calo Superfund site is in the Kingsbury Industrial Development Park; past site uses include the Kingsbury Ordnance Plant; Indiana and EPA found soil and groundwater contamination; a 2022 decision documented institutional controls to prevent exposure to contaminated groundwater.
sources.who: U.S. EPA, Superfund Sites in Reuse in Indiana

sources.what: Remnants of the plant are still visible; Kingsford Heights is 'the adjacent town'.
sources.who: Jeff Kenney, Towne Post (Lakes Region), 'Victory City' (2022)
